fetched_contents.text: Effects of bystander programs on the prevention of sexual assault among adolescents and college students: A systematic review - Kettrey - 2019 - Campbell Systematic Reviews 1 PLAIN LANGUAGE SUMMARY 1.1 Bystander programs increase bystander intervention but no effect on perpetrating sexual assault Bystander sexual assault prevention programs have beneficial effects on bystander intervention but there is no evidence of effects on sexual assault perpetration. Effects on knowledge and attitudes are inconsistent across outcomes. 1.2 What is this review about? Sexual assault is a significant problem among adolescents and college students across the world. One promising strategy for preventing these assaults is the implementation of bystander sexual assault prevention programs, which encourage young people to intervene when witnessing incidents or warning signs of sexual assault. This review examines the effects bystander programs have on knowledge and attitudes concerning sexual assault and bystander behavior, bystander intervention when witnessing sexual assault or its warning signs, and participants’ rates of perpetration of sexual assault. What is the aim of this review? This Campbell systematic review examines the effects of bystander programs on knowledge and attitudes concerning sexual assault and bystander intervention, bystander intervention when witnessing sexual assault or its warning signs, and the perpetration of sexual assault. The review summarizes evidence from 27 high-quality studies, including 21 randomized controlled trials. 2 WHAT ARE THE MAIN FINDINGS OF THIS REVIEW? 2.1 What studies are included? This review includes studies that evaluate the effects of bystander programs for young people on (a) knowledge and attitudes concerning sexual assault and bystander intervention, (b) bystander intervention behavior when witnessing sexual assault or its warning signs, and (c) perpetration of sexual assault. Twenty-seven studies met the inclusion criteria. These included studies span the period from 1997 to 2017 and were primarily conducted in the USA (one study was conducted in Canada and one in India). Twenty-one studies were randomized controlled trials and six were high quality quasi-experimental studies. 2.2 Do bystander programs have an effect on knowledge/attitudes, on bystander intervention, or on sexual assault perpetration? Bystander programs have an effect on knowledge and attitudes for some outcomes. The most pronounced beneficial effects are on rape myth acceptance and bystander efficacy outcomes. There are also delayed effects (i.e., 1 to 4 months after the intervention) on taking responsibility for intervening/acting, knowing strategies for intervening, and intentions to intervene outcomes. There is little or no evidence of effects on gender attitudes, victim empathy, date rape attitudes, and on noticing sexual assault outcomes. Bystander programs have a beneficial effect on bystander intervention. There is no evidence that bystander programs have an effect on participants’ rates of sexual assault perpetration. 3 WHAT DO THE FINDINGS OF THIS REVIEW MEAN? The United States 2013 Campus Sexual Violence Elimination (SaVE) Act requires postsecondary educational institutions participating in Title IX financial aid programs to provide incoming college students with sexual violence prevention programming that includes a component on bystander intervention. Bystander programs have a significant effect on bystander intervention. But there is no evidence that these programs have an effect on rates of sexual assault perpetration. This suggests that bystander programs may be appropriate for targeting the behavior of potential bystanders but may not be appropriate for targeting the behavior of potential perpetrators. Beneficial effects of bystander programs on bystander intervention were diminished by 6 months post-intervention. Thus, booster sessions may be needed to yield any sustained effects. There are still important questions worth further exploration. Namely, more research is needed to investigate the underlying causal mechanisms of program effects on bystander behavior (e.g., to model relationships between specific knowledge/attitude effects and bystander intervention effects), and to identify the most effective types of bystander programs (e.g., using randomized controlled trials to compare the effects of two alternate program models). Additionally, more research is needed in contexts outside of the USA so that researchers can better understand the role of bystander programs across the world. 4 HOW UP-TO-DATE IS THIS REVIEW? The review authors searched for studies up to June 2017. Published in final edited form as: Psychol Violence. 2022 Feb 14;12(6):403–412. doi: 10.1037/vio0000413 Abstract Objective: Most studies of peer sexual violence (SV) prevention programs for adolescents focus on program outcomes or feasibility and acceptability; few examine how exposure levels or dosage affects impact. The present study examined the effects of attending multiple community-located youth-led prevention events, as compared to attending one or none, on peer violence (PV)-related attitudes and behaviors. Method: Middle and high school students (Mage at first wave = 13.7; 53.2% female; 76.5% White; 21.0% Native American) responded to surveys across 3 years. Logistic regression analyses compared students who attended one community-based event, two or more events, and zero events on sexual violence victimization, any other violence perpetration/victimization, social norms, denial of the problem of sexual violence, and bystander behaviors. Results: After controlling for exposure to longer prevention leadership training as well as baseline outcome levels, youth who participated in two or more community prevention events showed lower perpetration over time, improved prevention attitudes, and more helpful bystander actions in response to peer sexual violence. No significant differences were noted for attendance at one community-based event. Conclusions: Impact of out of school prevention events on youth behavior depends on more vigorous engagement than one-time contacts. Community-based prevention programs can utilize youth-led engagement strategies to help increase youth participation and resulting benefits. Keywords: peer violence prevention, dosage, youth-led, leadership ---------------------------------------- Sexual violence (SV) and co-occurring forms of interpersonal violence, including dating violence, sexual harassment, and bullying by peers (referred to collectively as peer violence, or PV), are important public health problems among adolescents. National Youth Risk Behavior Survey (YRBS) data indicate that one in four adolescents report bullying victimization, one in eight report dating violence victimization, and one in ten report sexual violence victimization in the past year (Centers for Disease Control & Prevention, 2019). Prevention programs developed in response to violence among youth have shown important impacts on decreasing perpetration and victimization by changing intermediate outcomes, such as bystander intervention and violence supporting attitudes (Coker et al., 2019; Edwards et al., 2019; Foshee et al., 2005; Miller et al., 2013; Niolon et al., 2019). The majority of these programs take place in schools and are designed and implemented by adults; there are fewer studies of programs that take place in community spaces and that are youth-led (Edwards et al., 2016). These studies provide important foundational knowledge, but focus mainly on the broad question of whether the programs work. The present study explores a community-based prevention program and explores questions about the impact of dose, a facet of implementation. Specifically, the present study examined the impact of participation in zero events versus one event and two or more community peer sexual violence prevention events on adolescents’ prevention attitudes and behaviors, including bystander intervention, victimization, and perpetration. Implementation science reminds us that there are many barriers to the successful and ongoing use of prevention strategies in communities and different aspects of programs that may be more or less important for leveraging change (Wandersman et al., 2008). One key aspect of implementation is dose needed to produce effects, including the minimum dose of a prevention intervention required to produce intended impacts (Johnson et al., 2018; Proctor et al., 2015). While studies of these variables are common in topics, such as substance use prevention, there are few related to PV prevention, though it is noted as a key question for this field (Banyard et al., 2018; Davidov et al., 2019; Mihalic & Irwin, 2003). A number of implementation frameworks exist for understanding the conditions under which a prevention program is effective (Proctor et al., 2011) and dose of prevention needed is a key factor (Rowbotham et al., 2019). Dose has been conceptualized both in terms of how much of a program is delivered, or, alternately, how much prevention a participant was exposed to, and has been described as a component of fidelity (Dusenbury et al., 2003). In violence prevention, longer programs tend to produce greater effects, as do programs that include booster sessions to enhance dose (Banyard et al., 2007). Sustainability is also a key implementation outcome, as most prevention practitioners hope that if a strategy is successful, it will be maintained over time. Recent work by Johnson et al. (2018) noted that a depression prevention program’s sustainability may be enhanced by better understanding the minimum program dose needed to produce effects. Dose effects are noted by Nation et al. (2003) in their review of effective components of prevention initiatives. Furthermore, studies of PV prevention show enhanced effects of booster sessions and combined prevention tools (Banyard et al., 2018; Bundy et al., 2011). Yet, given that additional resources are needed to implement such booster sessions and increased doses, it is important to examine whether added effects are gained from multiple, compared to one, follow-up prevention activity. fetched_contents.text: An Online Bystander Intervention Program for the Prevention of Sexual Violence . Author manuscript; available in PMC: 2016 Jul 1. Published in final edited form as: Psychol Violence. 2014 Aug 11;5(3):227–235. doi: 10.1037/a0037393 Abstract Objective Because of its high prevalence and serious consequences for victims, sexual violence is a significant problem on college campuses. Sexual assault prevention programs based on the bystander intervention model have been shown to be effective; however, current programs are limited in terms of ease of distribution. To address this issue, we developed and evaluated “Take Care,” an online bystander intervention program. To our knowledge, this is the first empirical evaluation of an online bystander intervention program designed to prevent sexual violence. Method Ninety-three participants (80.6% female, 19.4% male) recruited from social psychology classes at a mid-size university were randomly assigned to view one of two online programs: Take Care or a control program on study skills. Before viewing the programs, participants completed measures of bystander behaviors and feelings of efficacy for performing such behaviors. Measures were administered again post-intervention and at a two-month follow-up assessment. Results Participants who viewed Take Care reported greater efficacy for engaging in bystander behaviors at post-treatment and two months following treatment, compared to those who viewed the control program. In addition, participants who viewed Take Care reported performing relatively more bystander behaviors for friends at the two-month follow-up assessment, compared to participants who viewed the control program. Conclusions These results suggest that sexual violence prevention programs may be effectively adapted to an online format. Keywords: bystander behavior, online intervention, sexual violence, college students, prevention programs ---------------------------------------- Sexual violence, which includes both sexual coercion and assault, is a significant problem on college campuses due to its high prevalence and adverse consequences. Estimates from surveys of college students indicate that 19–25% of women experience sexual violence while they are in college (Fisher, Cullen, & Turner, 2000; Krebs, Lindquist, Warner, Fisher, & Martin, 2009). Victims of sexual violence are at increased risk for a variety of adjustment difficulties, including trauma symptoms, eating disorders, diminished academic performance, and abuse of drugs and alcohol (Banyard & Cross, 2008; Stewart, Sebastiani, Delgado, & Lopez, 1996). Although numerous colleges have introduced programs to prevent sexual violence, and many incorporate such programs into their standard orientation curricula, their record of success in reducing the prevalence of sexual victimization on college campuses is poor (Casey & Nurius, 2006). Some have suggested that this may be due to shortcomings of the programs themselves (Anderson & Whiston, 2005; Antle, Sullivan, Dryden, Karam, & Barbee, 2011; Ferguson, San Miguel, Kilburn, & Sanchez, 2007; Yeater & O’Donohue, 1999). The present research evaluates a novel prevention program, which is designed to address some of shortcoming of existing programs and change behaviors that can potentially reduce the prevalence of sexual violence on college campuses. The majority of college sexual violence prevention programs include a focus on warning participants about the penalties for perpetrating sexual assault, or teaching participants skills for reducing victimization risk. Such programs may fail to engage their target audience, however, because individual students may not consider themselves to be a potential perpetrator or at particular risk for victimization (Foubert, Langhinrichsen-Rohling, Brasfield, & Hill, 2010; Potter, Krider, & McMahon, 2000). To overcome this, several program developers have taken another approach, targeting students not as potential victims or perpetrators, but rather as agents whose actions can reduce the risk that sexual violence will be committed by others, toward others. In programs using this approach, the responsibility for reducing sexual violence is thus extended beyond the victim-perpetrator dyad, to include the entire campus community. Such programs are commonly grounded in what is known as the bystander intervention model. Bystander interventions for sexual assault prevention are based, in part, on the early work of Darley and Latané (1968), who identified the “bystander effect” and factors that decrease bystanders’ willingness to intervene when they witness sexual violence or high-risk situations (i.e., those that might result in sexual violence). Bystander intervention programs aim to decrease sexual violence by increasing bystanders’ efficacy and willingness to engage in behaviors to deter potential sexual assault and to come to the aid of a victim—or potential victim—of sexual assault. Examples of such behaviors include walking a person home from a party who has had too much to drink or confronting a person seen drugging another person’s drink. Increasing bystander behaviors throughout a campus community is theorized to create a safer environment that is less tolerant of sexual coercion and violence. Many bystander intervention programs attempt to promote bystander behaviors by addressing theorized barriers to engaging in such behaviors. These barriers include, but are not limited to: failing to recognize or identify high-risk situations for sexual violence, not knowing what to say or do to intervene in high-risk situations, and not feeling a sense of responsibility for intervening (thinking that it is “none of my business” or that someone else should intervene) (Burn, 2009). Evidence and effectiveness comparison: adolescent programs, college programs, and bystander programs overall

The evidence base indicates that bystander programs are generally effective at improving knowledge, attitudes, and bystander behaviors, but less consistent on sexual assault perpetration and long-term durability. The Campbell systematic review found that bystander programs “have beneficial effects on bystander intervention” and “no evidence of effects on sexual assault perpetration,” while effects on knowledge and attitudes were inconsistent across outcomes [N3-F1]. It also reported delayed effects lasting 1 to 4 months after intervention on taking responsibility for intervening, knowing strategies for intervening, and intentions to intervene, but that these beneficial effects were diminished by 6 months post-intervention, suggesting the need for booster sessions [N3-F1].

Short-term outcomes appear stronger for bystander intervention and related attitudes. The same review states that the most pronounced beneficial effects are on rape myth acceptance and bystander efficacy outcomes, and that delayed effects were present for taking responsibility for intervening, knowing strategies for intervening, and intentions to intervene [N3-F1]. In the adolescent-specific evidence, a community-based youth-led prevention program found that students who attended two or more community prevention events showed lower perpetration over time, improved prevention attitudes, and more helpful bystander actions, whereas one event showed no significant differences [N4-F3]. This supports the idea that short-term and mid-term outcomes can be stronger when exposure is more frequent or intense.

College-specific evidence also suggests short-term efficacy, but with mixed durability. The online bystander intervention study found that participants who viewed the Take Care program reported greater efficacy for engaging in bystander behaviors at post-treatment and at a two-month follow-up assessment, and also reported performing relatively more bystander behaviors for friends at the two-month follow-up [N5-F4]. However, the review notes that bystander programs may not be appropriate for targeting sexual assault perpetration and that effects can diminish over time, with booster sessions needed to sustain them [N3-F1]. The college-specific evidence also points to limitations: some existing programs are criticized for poor success in reducing campus sexual violence prevalence, and a multi-college evaluation is described as the first to examine sexual and other interpersonal violence outcomes at the population level over time [N5-R4].

Moderators matter substantially. Age and setting are important. The review explicitly says that effects on knowledge/attitudes, bystander intervention, and perpetration should be interpreted in the context of age, setting, and measurement [N3-F1]. The adolescent program was conducted in middle and high school students and relied on repeated exposure to community-based events, while the college program was delivered online and included a control condition for comparison [N4-F3][N5-F4]. The college setting also has broader institutional demands, including orientation curricula and campus-wide implementation, which may shape effectiveness and scalability [N5-F4]. The Campbell review further emphasizes that more research is needed outside the USA and in different contexts to understand how bystander programs work across cultures and settings [N3-F1].

Overall, the evidence suggests that both adolescent and college bystander programs can produce stronger short-term outcomes in bystander efficacy, intentions, and helpful behaviors, but long-term outcomes are less robust and may depend on booster sessions or repeated exposure. Adolescents may benefit from community-based, youth-led, and dose-dependent interventions, while college students may be served by online, scalable, and campus-integrated formats. The strongest short-term outcomes are concentrated in bystander intervention and related attitudes, whereas sexual assault perpetration effects remain weak or absent [N3-F1][N4-F3][N5-F4].

Implementation and audience adaptation: adolescents versus college students

Programs are adapted differently for adolescents and college students, primarily through setting, delivery format, and the nature of engagement. The adolescent-specific evidence comes from a community-based youth-led prevention program called Youth Voices in Prevention (Youth VIP), which was delivered through multiple community prevention events rather than a single classroom or school-based session [N4-F3]. This suggests that adolescent programs are often designed to be embedded in community spaces and to leverage youth leadership, which may increase engagement and dose. The review also notes that these programs are often developed in schools but that fewer studies examine community-based or youth-led models [N4-F3].

In contrast, college-specific programs are more often delivered through online formats and campus-based interventions. The online bystander intervention study evaluated “Take Care,” an online program designed for college students, and found that it increased bystander efficacy and performed relatively more bystander behaviors at follow-up [N5-F4]. This reflects a format adaptation suited to college students’ access to digital tools and the need for scalable delivery. The college program also explicitly targets the campus community as a collective bystander audience, emphasizing that responsibility for reducing sexual violence is extended beyond the victim-perpetrator dyad [N5-F4].

Implementation barriers and facilitators differ by setting. For adolescents, a key barrier is reaching sufficient exposure; the Youth VIP study found that students who attended only one event showed no significant differences, whereas those who attended two or more events had stronger outcomes, indicating that dose and repeated engagement matter [N4-F3]. For college students, barriers include limited program effectiveness in reducing prevalence, and the review notes that current programs are limited in terms of ease of distribution [N5-F4]. Facilitators for college programs include online delivery, which can reach large audiences and reduce logistical burden, and campus integration into orientation curricula, which can support institutional buy-in [N5-F4].

Delivery formats vary by age group. Adolescents are more commonly served through community-based, multi-event, and youth-led formats, while college students are served through online interventions and campus-based programs [N4-F3][N5-F4]. The evidence also suggests that adolescent programs may rely on repeated community exposure, whereas college programs may emphasize online scalability and broader campus mobilization [N4-F3][N5-F4]. These differences in format reflect both developmental context and institutional context: adolescents are often engaged through out-of-school prevention events, while college students are often engaged through classroom, online, and campus-wide interventions [N4-F3][N5-F4].

Program design and intervention logic comparison

The evidence shows that bystander programs generally frame responsibility as collective rather than individual, and that the intervention logic is built around increasing awareness, reducing barriers, and promoting specific actions. The university bystander intervention page states that bystander intervention is a prevention strategy that encourages witnesses to take safe action when they see a situation that might lead to sexual violence or when someone is at risk for sexual assault [N1-R2]. The NSVRC bystander intervention toolkit similarly states that bystander intervention programs are designed to help build bystander knowledge, develop skills, decrease rape myths, and increase bystander self-efficacy [N2-R4]. This shared logic is also reflected in the broader literature, which frames the bystander approach as extending responsibility beyond the victim-perpetrator dyad and toward the entire campus community [N5-F4].

Gendered programs are explicitly framed through assumptions about power, responsibility, and masculinity. The Friends, Strangers, and Bystanders paper states that gendered ideas about physical power and violence are embedded within bystander prevention efforts themselves, and that “good” men are often called upon to protect women [N1-R2]. The same source also notes that bystander interventions train members of a community to develop awareness of situations where someone might need help, specifically where someone is at risk for sexual assault, and that responsibility is tied to these gendered understandings [N1-R2][N1-R3]. The NSVRC overview also emphasizes decreasing rape myths and increasing bystander self-efficacy, which implies that gendered language and assumptions are used to reshape attitudes about who should act and how those actions are justified [N2-R2][N2-R4].

Gender-neutral programs, by contrast, are framed around broader bystander responsibility and inclusivity. The NSVRC overview and toolkit emphasize bystander knowledge, skills, and self-efficacy without foregrounding gendered assumptions in the same way [N2-R2][N2-R4]. The college bystander intervention study explicitly targets students not as potential victims or perpetrators but as agents whose actions can reduce the risk that sexual violence will be committed by others toward others [N5-F4]. This framing broadens the audience and shifts responsibility away from a narrow gendered script. The evidence also suggests that gender-neutral approaches may be more explicitly designed to reduce rape myths and increase bystander efficacy, while gendered approaches may rely more on gendered norms and roles [N2-R4][N5-F4].

Differences in messaging, language, and assumed audience norms are clear. Gendered programs often use language tied to protecting women, assigning responsibility to “good” men, and addressing rape myths that are gendered [N1-R2][N2-R4]. Gender-neutral programs use language that is broader, more inclusive, and less reliant on fixed gender roles, such as “bystander,” “intervene,” “help,” and “campus community” [N1-R2][N2-R2][N5-F4]. The assumed audience norms also differ: gendered programs often assume a traditional gendered power structure, while gender-neutral programs assume a more collective and inclusive community responsibility [N1-R2][N5-F4]. The evidence does not provide a direct head-to-head comparison of effectiveness across these framing styles in the provided materials, but it does show that framing choices shape how responsibility is assigned and how bystander behavior is encouraged [N1-R2][N2-R2][N2-R4][N5-F4].

Gendered versus gender-neutral framing and language effects

The evidence indicates that gender framing can influence perceived responsibility and bystander efficacy, but the direction and strength of the effect are not fully resolved in the provided material. The Friends, Strangers, and Bystanders paper explicitly states that gendered ideas about physical power and violence are embedded in bystander prevention efforts, and that “good” men are called upon to protect women [N1-R2]. This suggests that gender framing can sharpen perceived responsibility, especially for men, by positioning them as expected interveners. The NSVRC overview also notes that bystander intervention programs are designed to decrease rape myths and increase bystander self-efficacy [N2-R2][N2-R4], implying that framing can affect both belief systems and self-efficacy.

The same evidence also suggests that gender framing may narrow participation by reinforcing exclusive gender roles. The paper states that gendered ideas about physical power and violence are embedded in the prevention efforts themselves, and that bystander interventions train members of a community to develop awareness of situations where someone might need help [N1-R2]. This framing can make participation feel contingent on gendered assumptions rather than on universal bystander norms. The college bystander intervention study, by contrast, explicitly targets students not as potential victims or perpetrators but as agents whose actions can reduce the risk that sexual violence will be committed by others toward others [N5-F4]. That approach broadens the audience and reduces reliance on fixed gender roles.

Evidence on inclusivity versus exclusivity in messaging is mixed but suggestive. Gender-neutral language and broader framing appear to support inclusivity by extending responsibility to the entire campus community rather than to a particular gendered role [N5-F4]. The NSVRC overview emphasizes bystander knowledge, skills, and self-efficacy without foregrounding gendered assumptions in the same way [N2-R2][N2-R4]. The evidence also indicates that gender-neutral approaches may be better suited to reducing rape myths and increasing bystander efficacy, while gendered approaches are more tied to traditional power and responsibility norms [N1-R2][N2-R4]. However, the provided evidence does not offer a direct comparison of whether gender-neutral language produces stronger inclusivity effects than gendered language, so any claim about inclusivity versus exclusivity remains tentative [N1-R2][N2-R2][N2-R4].

Overall, the evidence supports the idea that gender framing influences perceived responsibility and bystander efficacy, with gendered framing often reinforcing exclusive gender roles and gender-neutral framing broadening community responsibility [N1-R2][N2-R2][N2-R4][N5-F4]. The provided evidence does not establish a definitive superiority of one framing over the other, but it does show that framing choices shape both the logic of intervention and the likely audience response [N1-R2][N2-R4][N5-F4].

## Integrated final answer: how gendered and gender-neutral bystander programs differ in their approaches to preventing sexual assault among adolescents and college students

Bystander programs are designed to prevent sexual assault by encouraging witnesses to take safe action when they see a situation that might lead to sexual violence or when someone is at risk for sexual assault [N1-R2]. Across the evidence, gendered and gender-neutral programs differ mainly in how they frame bystander roles and responsibility, how they use language, and how they adapt to age and setting. The overall evidence also suggests that bystander programs are effective at improving knowledge, attitudes, and bystander behavior, but their long-term effects are less durable and may depend on booster sessions or repeated exposure [N3-F1].

---

## 1. Program design and intervention logic: responsibility, roles, and framing

### Gendered programs
Gendered bystander programs are often framed through assumptions about power, responsibility, and gender roles. The evidence states that gendered ideas about physical power and violence are embedded in bystander prevention efforts, and that “good” men are often called upon to protect women [N1-R2]. This framing positions men as expected interveners in a traditional gendered script, while women are framed as those in need of protection [N1-R2]. The same source also notes that bystander interventions train members of a community to develop awareness of situations where someone might need help, specifically where someone is at risk for sexual assault, and that responsibility is tied to these gendered understandings [N1-R2][N1-R3]. The NSVRC overview further emphasizes decreasing rape myths and increasing bystander self-efficacy, which reinforces the idea that gendered programs reshape attitudes and beliefs through gendered language and assumptions [N2-R2][N2-R4].

### Gender-neutral programs
By contrast, gender-neutral programs are framed around broader bystander responsibility and inclusivity. The NSVRC overview and toolkit emphasize bystander knowledge, skills, and self-efficacy without foregrounding gendered assumptions in the same way [N2-R2][N2-R4]. The college bystander intervention study explicitly targets students not as potential victims or perpetrators but as agents whose actions can reduce the risk that sexual violence will be committed by others toward others [N5-F4]. This shifts responsibility away from a narrow gendered script and toward the entire campus community [N5-F4]. The evidence also suggests that gender-neutral approaches may be more explicitly designed to reduce rape myths and increase bystander efficacy, while gendered approaches are more tied to traditional power and responsibility norms [N2-R4][N5-F4].

### Differences in messaging, language, and assumed audience norms
The key difference in messaging and language is whether programs rely on gendered norms or broader community norms. Gendered programs often use language tied to protecting women and assigning responsibility to “good” men [N1-R2]. Gender-neutral programs use language that is broader, more inclusive, and less reliant on fixed gender roles, such as “bystander,” “intervene,” “help,” and “campus community” [N1-R2][N2-R2][N5-F4]. Assumed audience norms also differ: gendered programs often assume a traditional gendered power structure, while gender-neutral programs assume a more collective and inclusive community responsibility [N1-R2][N5-F4]. In short, gendered programs can sharpen perceived responsibility but also reinforce exclusive gender roles; gender-neutral programs broaden participation and reduce reliance on fixed gender roles [N1-R2][N2-R2][N2-R4][N5-F4].

---

## 2. Evidence and effectiveness: what works, when, and for whom

### Short-term outcomes
Across the evidence base, bystander programs show stronger short-term outcomes on bystander intervention, knowledge, attitudes, and related behaviors. The Campbell systematic review found that bystander programs have beneficial effects on bystander intervention and that the most pronounced beneficial effects were on rape myth acceptance and bystander efficacy outcomes [N3-F1]. ### Long-term outcomes

The Campbell review explicitly states that beneficial effects on bystander intervention were diminished by 6 months post-intervention and that booster sessions may be needed to yield sustained effects [N3-F1]. The adolescent program also suggests that repeated exposure is important for sustained change, because students who attended only one event showed no significant differences [N4-F3]. The college-specific evidence similarly indicates that bystander programs may not be appropriate for targeting sexual assault perpetration and that effects can diminish over time [N3-F1][N5-F4].

The review explicitly says that effects on knowledge/attitudes, bystander intervention, and perpetration should be interpreted in the context of age, setting, and measurement [N3-F1]. Adolescents are often served through community-based, multi-event, and youth-led formats, while college students are often served through online interventions and campus-based programs [N4-F3][N5-F4]. ## 3. Implementation and audience adaptation: adolescents versus college students

### How programs are adapted
Adolescent programs are adapted through community-based, youth-led, and dose-dependent designs. The adolescent-specific evidence comes from a community-based youth-led prevention program called Youth Voices in Prevention (Youth VIP), which was delivered through multiple community prevention events rather than a single classroom or school-based session [N4-F3]. The Friends, Strangers, and Bystanders paper explicitly states that gendered ideas about physical power and violence are embedded in bystander prevention efforts, and that “good” men are called upon to protect women [N1-R2]. ### How gender-neutral language may broaden or narrow participation
